blocks.c: Chapter Twenty: Tamsin's Last Round
There is a thing bell-hands are told and do not believe, which is that a cracked bell can be rung.

Not safely. Not twice. A cracked bell will give you one true tail if you strike it exactly right — on the sound-bow, square, at the one point on the circumference where the fault is not — and it will hum for perhaps eleven seconds, and then the crack will run the rest of the way and the bell will be scrap and the sound will come out of it in a way that no ear should be within twenty feet of.
Roake sent Sol for the plate.

It was in the bell-master's cubby, under the tally: a curved iron plate on a chain, the width of a hand, four hundred years old, called a hush. You clamp it over the crack to hold the metal together for the length of one strike. Every ship carried one. Nobody had used one in living memory. Sol had been shown it once, at thirteen, along with the fire buckets and the ballast wrench, in the tour where you are shown all the things that mean everything has gone wrong.

She came back up the nineteen rungs with the plate in her teeth, and on the way she passed a steward going down with an armful of blankets, and the steward said something to her that she did not hear, and she thought afterwards that it had probably been good luck, and that she should have answered.
That is what those minutes were like. Everybody doing their own small correct thing in a ship that was going down, and none of it adding up to enough, and all of it necessary.

The Gull was down thirty-one spans and falling slower, held on three deep bells and a stolen twin, and the cloud-tops were no longer below them; they were level, and coming past the gallery in long grey fingers.
"Give it here," said Roake.
"Bosun—"
"Ferrant, give me the plate."
"You'll be next to it."
"Yes."
"You'll be a foot from it when it goes—"
"Yes," said Tamsin Roake, and took the hush out of her hands.
She clamped it. She checked it with her thumb, twice, the way she checked everything, and Sol saw her mouth moving and could not hear a word over the wind.
"Ferrant. Off the gallery."
"No."
"That was not a request, it was an order, and I am the bell-master."

"And I'm the ear," said Sol, "and if that hush slips a hair you'll not know it and I will, and I can shout at you from the number-eight cradle, which is eleven feet, which is further than you're going to be." Her voice was doing something appalling. "Bosun, please. Let me be useful. Don't make me be a witness."
Tamsin Roake looked at her for about a second and a half, which in the circumstances was an enormous extravagance.
"Number-eight cradle," she said. "Behind the yoke. Hands over your ears from the ninth strike and do not take them down for anything."

Then Roake looked down the line of nine bells — eight good and one dying — and she did the thing that Sol thought about every day for the rest of her life, which was that she took the time to walk the line and touch each cradle, in order, bow to stern, the superstition that everyone on that ship pretended not to have.
Then she rang the round.
Keel, low and enormous. Ladder. Kestrel. Quarrel. Mother, taking her breath and then saying everything at once. Lantern. Thimble. Widow, sour and reliable.
Four and one. Four and one. Not one strike out.

And at the stern, with her left hand flat on the hush and her right on the hammer, at a distance from a failing bell that no bell-master in four hundred years had survived and gone on hearing, Tamsin Roake struck the Ninth of the Meridian Gull.
It rang true.

It rang true for eleven seconds, and in those eleven seconds Sol Ferrant felt the carry come back into the frame under her hands like water into a dry channel, felt the whole eight hundred tons of the ship stop arguing with the sky and lie down on it, felt the Gull come up four spans, then four more; and four hundred feet below, a nineteen-year-old called Pel, whose town had eleven seconds of carry left in it, heard his ship's ninth bell speak and knew he could stop.
Then the crack ran.

The noise that came out of the Ninth was not a sound. Sol was eleven feet away and she went down on the plating with her hands over her ears and it did not help; it came through her forearms. Dov, at the frame, was knocked flat. The hush plate tore off its chain and went out over the rail into the cloud and was never found.
And Tamsin Roake, one foot from the bell she had kept for twenty-two years, did not move at all until it was over.

The Gull came up nineteen spans in four minutes and levelled at thirty-one, and the squall went over the top of her and away south, and four hundred and eleven passengers were told by a purser of forty-one years' standing that there had been an incident with a bell, that the ship was safe, that the bar would be open and free until Antrell, and that anybody who wished to make a complaint should address it to him personally and in writing, which is the single most effective method ever devised for reducing the number of complaints.

She was standing when Sol got to her. Standing, with her hand still on the hammer, looking at the ruined bell with a kind of professional sorrow, and when Sol grabbed her arm she turned round and her face was perfectly calm.
Sol was shouting. She knew she was shouting. She could hear herself shouting.
Roake watched her mouth for a moment. Then she reached out and put her palm flat against Sol's breastbone, over the sternum, where the underhum lives, and held it there.
"Don't shout," she said, far too loudly, in the voice of a person who cannot hear their own voice. "It doesn't work anymore."
She looked past Sol, down the line of bells, at eight good iron hearts and one dead one, and at a ship that was rising.
"Ferrant," said the bell-master of the Meridian Gull. "Tally."
